Newborn Care

Newborn Development: The First Three Months

Updated: July 1, 2026

In three short months, your baby transforms from a curled-up newborn running on reflexes into a smiling, cooing little person who knows your face. Development in this window is rapid but wonderfully low-tech to support , no flashcards required, just you. Here is what unfolds and how to encourage it.

Born with reflexes

Newborns arrive with a built-in toolkit of reflexes: rooting (turning toward a cheek touch to find food), sucking, grasping a finger placed in the palm, the startle (Moro) reflex with its dramatic arm fling, and stepping motions when held upright on a surface.

These automatic responses are signs of a healthy nervous system, and most fade over the first months as deliberate, controlled movement takes over. Your pediatrician checks them at well-baby visits.

How newborn senses work

Newborn vision is blurry beyond about 20–30 centimeters (8–12 inches) , conveniently, the distance to your face during a feed. Babies prefer faces and high-contrast patterns, and over these months they learn to track moving objects and see a wider range of color.

Hearing is well developed at birth, and your baby already prefers your voice from months of hearing it. Smell and touch are strong too , which is why your scent and skin-to-skin contact are so calming.

Tummy time: tiny workouts

Tummy time , placing your awake, supervised baby on their front , builds the neck, shoulder, and core strength behind every later milestone from rolling to crawling. It also helps prevent flat spots on the back of the head.

Start early with a few minutes, a couple of times a day, and build up as your baby gets stronger. If your baby protests, try shorter sessions, lay them on your chest while you recline, or get down face-to-face and chat , company changes everything. Always tummy time awake and watched; always sleep on the back.

The first social smile

Somewhere around six to eight weeks, the fleeting sleep-smiles give way to the real thing: a social smile aimed at you, in response to your face and voice. It is one of the great paydays of early parenting.

Cooing follows close behind, and by three months many babies are having full "conversations" of coos, gurgles, and grins. Answering these , pausing, replying, taking turns , is exactly how communication skills are built.

A month-by-month sketch

Month one is mostly reflexes, feeding, and brief alert windows , with your baby studying faces up close and turning toward familiar voices. Head control is minimal, so keep supporting that neck.

Month two brings smoother movements, longer alert stretches, early cooing, better head control during tummy time, and those first genuine social smiles.

By month three, many babies hold their head steadier, push up on forearms during tummy time, bat at and briefly hold objects, track people across the room, and laugh or squeal. Remember these are typical ranges, not deadlines , healthy babies vary widely.

Everyday interaction is the curriculum

Nothing supports newborn development like ordinary, responsive interaction: talking and narrating your day, singing, reading aloud (the story does not matter, the voice does), making eye contact, and responding to coos and cries.

Variety helps too , different rooms, a walk outside, safe household objects to look at, and plenty of floor time instead of long stretches in seats and swings. If you ever feel your baby is losing skills or consistently missing milestones, raise it with your pediatrician; early questions are always worth asking.

Key takeaways

  • Newborn reflexes , rooting, grasping, startle , are healthy and fade as control develops.
  • Babies see best at 20–30 cm and prefer faces; your voice is already their favorite sound.
  • Daily supervised tummy time builds the strength behind all later milestones.
  • Social smiles arrive around 6–8 weeks, with cooing conversations soon after.
  • Talking, singing, reading, and responding are the best development tools , milestones are ranges, not deadlines.

Frequently asked questions

When should I start tummy time?

You can start in the first weeks , even a few minutes at a time, a couple of times a day, while your baby is awake and supervised. Build up gradually as neck strength grows.

My baby has not smiled yet , should I worry?

Social smiles typically appear around six to eight weeks, but the normal range is wide. If there is no social smiling by around three months, or you have other concerns, mention it at a well-baby visit , asking early is always reasonable.

Do I need special toys to support development?

No. In the first three months, your face, voice, and attention outperform any toy. High-contrast images and simple safe objects are nice extras, but everyday talking, singing, and cuddling do the heavy lifting.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
